strengths: Originality: The contribution is a useful statistical analysis connecting pixel resolution, template deformation, and classification error. Linking these quantities to deformation covering numbers provides meaningful understanding beyond proposing another invariant representation.

Significance and technical merits: The explicit alignment and inverse-mapping classifiers provide useful theoretical benchmarks. Their analysis explains why, under suitable separation and visibility conditions, observing one example from each class can suffice.

Presentation: The progression from simple transformations to general deformations and CNN classifiers is clear. Illustrations, explicit assumptions, and extensive appendix derivations make the constructions accessible and permit detailed scrutiny.

Limitations and ethics: Sections 3.2 and 7 appropriately acknowledge difficulties involving background noise, occlusion, multiple objects, and sharp edges. These disclosures are constructive. The theoretical work and public benchmark examples raise no apparent material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness—CNN assumptions: Assumption 2(i) does not guarantee the support property repeatedly used in Proposition B.5. Containing the template rectangle in A([0,1]^2) implies full visibility only with additional restrictions on preimages. For example, A(u,v)=((1−cos(2πu))/2,v) has bounded continuous derivatives and maps the unit square onto itself, but a composed template repeats outside the image. Equations (89) and (101) require those outside copies to vanish; the change-of-variables equality in (90) also ignores multiplicity. Since Section 4 explicitly permits noninvertible deformations, the general CNN guarantees are unsupported as stated. Explicit support/preimage conditions or a restriction to invertible maps are needed.

Soundness—separation optimality: Theorem 3.8 establishes a lower bound on ordinary normalized L2 distance between templates, whereas the upper guarantees use distance minimized over transformations, as in (12) and (23). A lower bound before minimization does not establish a lower bound afterward. Consequently, the claimed matching 1/d separation threshold is not proved. The theorem also quantifies fixed templates before 'for any d,' although its construction makes the perturbed template depend on d.

Soundness—minimax interpretation: The generic VC lower bound cited after Theorem 4.4 does not establish minimax optimality within the proposed deformation model. The manuscript does not show that the distributions needed for that lower bound belong to this model. This distinction matters because Theorem 3.1 already establishes perfect classification after both labels are observed in the separated, invertible setting.

Significance and evaluation: Section 5 uses synthetic transformations of one selected template per class, including images with backgrounds removed. These are useful model illustrations, but provide limited evidence about classification across distinct object instances. The experiments do not directly test the central dependence on resolution, template separation, or deformation covering complexity. Reporting only median errors over ten repetitions, with 50 or 200 test images, also provides limited support for claims of vanishing error.

Reproducibility: The manuscript supplies no code link and omits essential experimental details, including template identifiers, deformation distributions and ranges, background-removal procedures, training epochs, batch sizes, and fully connected depth. Table 1 specifies filter sizes, filter counts, and widths only. It is also unclear whether the implementations enforce the normalization, parameter bounds, and clipped cross-entropy formulation used in the theory.

Presentation and positioning: Pages 19–20 incorrectly characterize existing generalization bounds, including [8,42], as applying only to functions independent of training data. Uniform bounds also apply to data-dependent learned networks. The manuscript should distinguish its distribution-specific approximation and convergence analysis without relying on this inaccurate account of prior work.
